svg.text: winfixup — a fault inside a register window spill
The one fault in the machine that cannot be handled where it happens. The answer is not to resume it; it is to abandon it and re-run the user's instruction.
HOW IT ARISES — NOTHING UNUSUAL IS REQUIRED
A save only moves the stack pointer. It writes nothing. So when a program recurses onto a stack page it has not used before,
the first thing to touch that page is the spill handler's own store — and the spill handler runs at trap level one.
Every program does this. A 300-deep recursion crosses six 8 KB pages and takes six of these faults, measured.
sparc: winfixup -- spill trap 0x84 abandoned at 0x7a4e4000, re-running pc 0x5e4f4214, thread 37
WHY IT CANNOT BE HANDLED IN PLACE
TL = 2 — the fault
an unmapped page under the spill's store
TL = 1 — the spill, still owed a retry
%tpc holds the user's save; CWP moved by the hardware
TL = 0 — userspace
where the C fault handler has to run
The trap registers are stacked per level
Handling a fault means reaching trap level zero, because C
must be able to take its own TLB misses. But dropping to zero
from here throws level one away — and level one is the only
record of where userspace was.
Nesting instead is worse: four levels reaches MAXTL and the
machine takes a watchdog reset, silently.
So the spill is not resumed. It is abandoned.
AND ABANDONING COSTS NOTHING, BECAUSE OF WHAT A SPILL TRAP ALREADY IS
A spill trap is taken instead of completing a save, and its handler ends in retry — which re-executes that same save,
whereupon a window is free and it succeeds. Re-running the user's instruction is not a workaround; it is the normal path.
And nothing needs undoing. saved and restored are the instructions that move the window accounting, and a handler
that faulted before reaching them changed only CWP — which the hardware moved, and which TSTATE still records.
THE FIXUP
1. Record
the address, from Tag
Access — with the context
shifted off, since that
register is not an address.
2. Drop to TL = 1
discarding the fault. The
window trap's registers are
untouched and describe a
user instruction.
3. Restore CWP
from TSTATE bits 4:0, to
the window the user's
instruction ran in. Safe
because nothing else moved.
4. Ordinary fault
The machine is now
indistinguishable from one
that took a data fault out
of userspace. C runs.
5. retry
re-runs the user's
save. The spill
happens again, against
a page that is there.
Why it cannot loop
An address that cannot be paged in raises SIGSEGV and the
thread dies. Every pass either makes the page present or
ends the thread.
Why it cannot recurse
Step 4's own save could spill — and used to spill to the
user's stack, at the same address. The trap entry now hands
the user's windows over before that save, so it cannot.
Trap level and window-state rules from the UltraSPARC-IIi User's Manual, chapters 5 and 6. Shape from Linux's arch/sparc/kernel/winfixup.S — behaviour only, no code; see THIRD_PARTY.md.
